case20v1-sol.ai.prototype:
Ashtam and the Ninety-Minute Prototype

A teaching case on AI-generated prototypes in product discovery

1. Opening

At 8.00 a.m. on Monday, 10 August 2026, Heena Lokapur sat in Ashtam's Baner office in Pune with a laptop open to a screen that did not yet exist as a product. On Monday 3 August she had typed a description of an idea into an AI app builder and, in under ninety minutes of prompting and correcting, produced a working prototype: a merchant could speak or type an invoice in Hindi, Marathi or English and see a finished GST invoice, then open a screen that reconciled purchases against the government's auto-drafted input tax credit statement.

Eighteen merchants had since tried it, and they had liked it. Heena, Ashtam's head of product, now had to tell the chief executive by Friday, 21 August, at the quarterly planning meeting, what the company should do next. Diwali fell on Sunday, 8 November, and small traders restock and buy software in the weeks before it. The question was not whether the prototype was impressive. It was what, exactly, it had proved.

2. Company background

Ashtam sells GST billing and bookkeeping software to small traders: kirana owners, hardware dealers, cloth wholesalers and distributors across Maharashtra, Gujarat and Madhya Pradesh. Founded in 2018, it had 62,000 paying merchants on a plan averaging ₹4,200 a year, an annual recurring revenue of ₹26.04 crore. Its competitors included Tally, Zoho Books, Vyapar, Khatabook, and the merchant apps of PhonePe and Paytm.

Ashtam's edge was vernacular support and a customer-success team that picked up the phone. GST compliance was the reason merchants bought, yet the monthly reconciliation of purchase invoices against the government's GSTR-2B statement remained an accountant's job, charged by the filing. An assistant that did it in plain language would be a new product line, pencilled in as a ₹399-a-month add-on, or ₹4,788 a year.

3. The situation

Heena's prototype ran on sample data for an invented trader. The invoice feature, however, used a live language model, so what merchants said was genuinely interpreted. On Wednesday 5 to Friday 7 August, Ashtam's customer-success team put it in front of 18 existing customers: seven in Pune, six in Surat and five in Indore. Exhibit 1 sets out what the sessions measured.

The first two rows were strong, and the fourth excited the sales team. The third was a warning: the model was right about three prompts in four, which is not good enough for an invoice a trader hands to a customer. The last row was the quietest and, Heena suspected, the most important: no merchant had seen a reconciliation figure that could be wrong, because none of the figures were theirs.

The team saw it from four places. In Bengaluru, Hrithik Lakkad, the engineering lead, had opened the generated code: roughly 1,900 lines, no tests, GST rates hard-coded. In Berlin, the designer, Henrike Lauber, had watched recordings and noticed that merchants treated the screen as finished software because it looked finished. Hardeep Lalvani, the sales head in New Jersey, wanted to show it to chartered-accountant partners. And Hasini Lokre, who ran customer success from Singapore, had run the sessions and worried about what came after. Berlin, Pune and Singapore overlapped only at 12.30 p.m. IST (9.00 a.m. in Berlin, 3.00 p.m. in Singapore) and Hardeep's evening was Heena's early morning, so most of the argument happened in writing.

4. The people

Hrithik Lakkad, engineering lead, Bengaluru. He wanted to take the prototype as the specification and build at once: ten weeks, six engineers. He saw more research as delay.

Henrike Lauber, product designer, Berlin. She wanted the next stage to test the hard states the prototype skipped: a mismatch the merchant disagrees with, an invoice the model misread, a month with no data.

Hardeep Lalvani, head of sales, New Jersey. He wanted something in front of accountant partners before the festive rush and thought a rough beta now beat a perfect release in December.

Hasini Lokre, customer-success lead, Singapore. She wanted nothing live until a human accountant had checked the numbers. A merchant who claimed credit the data did not support could lose it, and the complaint would reach her team.

5. Exhibits

Three options had taken shape, priced in Exhibit 2 at loaded weekly rates: ₹0.60 lakh for an engineer in Pune or Bengaluru, ₹1.10 lakh for the Berlin designer, ₹1.40 lakh for the Toronto data scientist, ₹0.90 lakh for the Singapore customer-success lead and ₹0.45 lakh for a Pune tester.

Figure 1. Timeline of the options. Scale: 8 pixels a day from 3 August 2026; the dashed line is Diwali, Sunday 8 November.

In Exhibit 2, money was not the constraint. Option A's ₹44.00 lakh is recovered in a year by 919 merchants paying ₹4,788, which is 1.48 per cent of the 62,000 base; five per cent, or 3,100 merchants, would yield ₹1.48 crore. Option C was cheap and early and, Hasini pointed out, put unchecked tax figures in merchants' hands soonest. Option B added about a week to the launch date compared with A, as Figure 1 shows.

6. The options

Option A: build the product now. Assign six engineers for ten weeks and launch on 30 October. The upside is the earliest full product. The cost is ₹44.00 lakh committed before reconciliation has been tested on a real merchant's data, the hardest part of the feature.

Option B: run a short learning cycle against a decision rule. For three weeks, give 40 consenting merchants a revised prototype wired to their live GSTR-2B data through a GST Suvidha Provider, with consent handled under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. Critique, revise and re-test weekly, then decide on 11 September against Exhibit 3. The upside is that the expensive risks are tested for ₹8.95 lakh. The cost is a week of launch time and a possible no.

Option C: ship the prototype as a paid beta. Fix the worst parsing errors and release it on 7 September to 150 merchants. It would produce real usage and revenue quickly, and Hardeep would have his demonstration. Against that, reconciliation figures would be live, the code has no tests, and a wrong credit claim harms the merchant.

7. Questions for discussion

1. Which rows of Exhibit 1 does the prototype prove, which does it only suggest, and which could it never have measured, given how it was built and who tested it?

2. Each colleague is partly right. What does the prototype give each of them evidence for, and what does it leave unanswered?

3. Option A's cost is recovered by 1.48 per cent of the base, yet Heena hesitates. What does that tell you about where the real risk in this decision sits?

4. Would you adopt the rule in Exhibit 3? Which threshold would you change, and what would you do if the first measure passed but the second failed?

8. A note for the learner

An AI-generated prototype answers a narrow question quickly: can this concept work on a screen, and will people grasp it? It does so in hours rather than weeks. It does not prove that the hard part works, because a prototype is built to look finished before it is true. The reconciliation screen scored 83.3 per cent on comprehension and was never checked for accuracy; both facts describe the same screen. The skill this topic teaches is separating what the artefact demonstrates from what its polish implies, then buying evidence for the second at the lowest price.

A well-reasoned answer therefore treats the prototype as a learning vehicle with a decision rule, not a small product. It names the riskiest assumption, here that Ashtam can reconcile a real merchant's real data correctly, and designs the next prototype to test that and nothing else. It also respects what the sample cannot say: eighteen invited customers and a stated willingness to pay tell the team little about the other 61,982 merchants.

One defensible path is Option B, with Hasini's condition built in: no merchant sees an unchecked figure, since an accountant confirms each flag. It keeps Hrithik's momentum, because the revised prototype and the logs from 40 merchants become a better specification than the original, and it gives Henrike the hard states she wanted. The cost is about a week of launch timing against the Diwali window, which is small next to the ₹44.00 lakh Option A would commit before the gate. Option A is not wrong in principle; it is early. Option C is weakest, because it ships the one thing the prototype never tested. Whichever option is chosen, Heena should say in advance what result would change her mind.

Lagori Systems and the Prototype That Sold Itself

For class discussion. Lagori Systems, Lamsa Markets, Lohagarh Foods and Lathe are fictitious; the market and institutions named are real.

1. Sunday night, Baner

At 10.20 p.m. on Sunday, 18 October 2026, Sanchita Ayachit sat in a service apartment in Baner, Pune, with two laptops open. She had flown up from Bengaluru, where she ran product for Lagori Systems Private Limited, for the board sub-committee at nine the next morning.

On the left-hand screen was a prompt she had written on 6 July: 1,420 words describing a supplier self-service portal, down to the field names. On the right was what that prompt and six follow-on prompts had become — a working web application, logged in as a fictitious Dubai spice trader, that filtered claims by invoice, showed a promotion calendar and produced a settlement statement reconciled to the paisa.

Two months earlier, in a Dubai workshop room, twenty-three of Lamsa Markets' category managers had taken turns driving that application. On 11 September Lamsa signed a letter of intent: a ten-week pilot from Monday, 2 November 2026 at a fee of ₹180 lakh, and a three-year licence at ₹6 crore a year if the pilot was accepted.

The settlement statement did not exist. Lathe, the prompt-to-application builder Lagori licensed by the seat, had written it against a seeded file: no rule engine, and settlement rules differ by contract. Sanchita had known this on 20 August and said so once, quietly, to the room. Sudarshan Agnihotri, the investor-director chairing Monday's meeting, had asked her on Friday for "a one-page recommendation, with the number you are betting the quarter on". She had not written it.

2. Lagori Systems, 2016–2026

Lagori was founded in Pune in 2016 by Sarosh Avachat, after eleven years building distributor software for a consumer-goods group. Its product does load-bearing work: order capture on a distributor salesman's phone, scheme and claim settlement between a brand and its channel, and reconciliation of both against GST e-invoices from the Invoice Registration Portal. By FY2026 it had 384 people, 64 in product engineering, and revenue of ₹138 crore (Exhibit 1), of which ₹8 crore came from outside India.

One decision from 2021 shapes what is available in 2026. To win Lohagarh Foods, still its largest customer, Sarosh agreed to deploy in Lohagarh's own data centre against a forked copy of the core schema, with Lohagarh's claim taxonomy written into the tables rather than into configuration. The deal took Lagori from ₹31 crore of revenue in FY2021 to ₹96 crore in FY2023. It set a precedent: eleven customers now run schema-forked, single-tenant deployments, so any new module must be built eleven times or wait behind a compatibility layer on the roadmap since 2024 and never staffed (Exhibit 6). Siddhesh Amonkar, VP Engineering since 2022, has twice called the forks "the interest payment on 2021".

3. The industry

Lagori sells into a channel being rearranged around it. Quick commerce — Zepto, Blinkit, Swiggy Instamart — has pulled urban grocery demand out of the distributor-to-kirana chain its software instruments, while Reliance Retail and DMart buy direct on their own terms. GST e-invoicing made reconciliation a statutory obligation with an audit trail, the best reason brands still pay Lagori rather than build; the DPDP Act, 2023 turned the contact data in its customers' tenants into a consent question, answered on the roadmap by a consent-ledger module.

Against Freshworks and Zoho it loses on breadth and wins on claim-settlement depth; against Infosys and TCS, which bid the same Gulf programmes, it loses on balance sheet and wins on time to first screen. The Gulf matters to Indian exporters — Amul and Tata Consumer brands sit on Gulf shelves — and Lamsa Markets, a Dubai grocery and hypermarket group with 108 stores in the UAE and Oman, buys from 96 active suppliers, a little over half of them Indian. It is also Lagori's first contract placing personal data of UAE residents in scope, which Lamsa's board policy requires be stored in the UAE.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

Lamsa's request for information arrived on 12 March 2026 and asked for a supplier portal in nine months. Lagori's April qualification call put the work at eighteen months of platform change and declined to bid. In June Sameer re-opened it: Sabiha Ajmera, Lamsa's group digital director, had told him her programme budget expired with Lamsa's financial year.

On 6 July Sanchita wrote the prompt. Svenja Arnholdt, Lagori's design lead in Berlin, ran it through Lathe and then six more prompts over eleven days, each narrower than the last. By 17 July there were fifteen screens, a login and data for forty fictitious suppliers (Exhibit 2). Three things believed then have not survived. First, that the build was a throwaway for a conversation: Siddhesh's review on 23 and 24 July found 1,680 of the 14,730 generated lines worth keeping, about 11 per cent — which hardly mattered, because what travelled to Dubai was the running application, not the code. Second, that the Arabic interface worked: the right-to-left layout was a mirrored stylesheet with transliterated labels: convincing on a projector, meaningless as localisation. Third, that the demo audience was the user. Lamsa's category managers are the portal's buyers; its users are the 96 suppliers, almost none of whom has seen it.

The workshop ran on Thursday, 20 August 2026: five tasks, twenty-three participants, recordings from Lathe's session recorder (Exhibit 3). Sameer's note to Sarosh reported "90 per cent task completion". The letter of intent was signed on 11 September. Between 1 and 12 September, Shruti Arondekar's team in Singapore tried to reach Lamsa's suppliers; that funnel, and the question added to the guide only on 7 September, are in Exhibit 4.

On 2 October Lamsa's procurement sent the payment schedule: ₹45 lakh of the ₹180 lakh pilot fee is payable only on acceptance of the reconciliation module — the screen Lathe invented. Nobody read the clause until 9 October. On 13 October Simran Adlakha, the Toronto data scientist preparing the board exhibit, sent Sameer's draft back with two corrections.

5. The people

Sanchita Ayachit, 36, VP Product, Bengaluru. Position: none in writing, which Sarosh has noticed. Incentive: an ESOP tranche on FY2027 new-logo revenue and a CPO title Sudarshan calls "next year's conversation". Not saying: she wrote the prompt that invented the reconciliation screen, and said nothing when Sabiha asked whether the settlement logic was configurable.

Sarosh Avachat, 52, co-founder and CEO, Pune. Position: take the deal; the logo outweighs the margin. Incentive: a Series C in which international revenue share is the slide investors stop at. Not saying: two of the three funds asked whether Lagori can deploy without a schema fork, and he said the layer is "in flight".

Siddhesh Amonkar, 41, VP Engineering, Pune. Position: rebuild on the core, take the February date, tell Lamsa now. Incentive: the forks are his to live with, and the layer would at last be funded by someone else's deal. Not saying: he put four engineers onto a claims rewrite on 28 September without a budget line — which is why Path B's estimate is firmer than it should be, and eight weeks of fork support has slipped.

Svenja Arnholdt, 33, design lead, Berlin. Position: the generated build is the specification; documents about software that already runs are theatre. Incentive: six more Lathe seats and a design team of her own. Not saying: the promotion-calendar flow came from an unshipped 2024 project of hers, so its fluency was no evidence that Lathe understood anything; and her contract ends on 31 January 2027.

Simran Adlakha, 29, data scientist, Toronto. Position: the telemetry cannot carry the claim made on it. Incentive: she is the one person whose standing improves when a number is withdrawn. Not saying: in nine of the twenty-three recordings she cannot tell whether the facilitator was driving, so her own unaided-versus-prompted split is softer than Exhibit 3's columns suggest.

Shruti Arondekar, 38, customer success lead, Singapore. Position: narrow the pilot to what Lagori can stand behind. Incentive: her renewal targets sit on the accounts whose roadmap items are being displaced. Not saying: Lohagarh's IT head has twice asked when the GST e-invoice 2.1 update lands, the second time using the word "escalate".

Sameer Ahluwalia, 45, head of sales, New Jersey. Position: sign, ship something, fix it in the pilot. Incentive: the licence lands in his FY2027 quota, and Lamsa is the reference that opens a US grocery chain. Not saying: that prospect's security review asks for the provenance of generated code, which he has not raised with Siddhesh.

Path B — rebuild on the core platform behind phase 1 of the compatibility layer. ₹248.7 lakh, fourteen weeks of build and a two-week cutover, go-live 8 February 2027. It funds the layer 2021 made necessary, and Siddhesh's four unauthorised engineers have begun it. It costs more than the pilot fee, needs fourteen engineers where twelve are uncommitted, and lands as Lamsa's peak season opens.

Path C — a read-only claims-visibility pilot in six weeks, with the generated build kept as the specification for the rest. ₹153.9 lakh against a fee Sabiha indicates would fall to ₹105 lakh. It is defensible, starts on 30 November rather than 2 November, and ships precisely the part that Exhibit 4b's five ERP-integrated suppliers said they do not need.

Sanchita has written all three on one sheet and finds it unsatisfying. Each takes the 2 November date and Lamsa's scope as fixed, and treats the prototype as an asset to be shipped, discarded or framed. None says what the pilot is for; none states a result that would make Lagori stop. And no path on the sheet is the one Shruti proposed on 15 October and nobody costed: put the build that already runs in front of twenty actual suppliers for two weeks before anyone writes anything. Lohagarh Foods and a durables group have each asked for the same portal, and have budget; that appears nowhere either.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The sub-committee meets at 9 a.m. on Monday, 19 October 2026. The letter of intent commits Lagori to a pilot from Monday, 2 November — the week of Diwali on 8 November, with both Indian offices at half strength — with a sixty-day termination right either side and ₹45 lakh of the ₹180 lakh fee payable only on acceptance of the reconciliation module. Lamsa's board policy requires supplier data to sit in the UAE; Lagori hosts in Mumbai, and the UAE footprint costs ₹36 lakh for twelve months on every path. Sabiha cannot take a cutover into the Ramadan trading peak, expected in the second week of February 2027.

Internally: 12 of 64 product engineers are uncommitted, against a displaced roadmap of 280 person-weeks and ₹11.70 crore of Indian ARR at renewal. Lathe's seats renew on 30 November at ₹5.04 lakh each, 40 per cent above the ₹3.60 lakh Lagori pays now, and Exhibit 5 prices every path at the new rate. Svenja's contract ends on 31 January 2027. Lagori held ₹41 crore of cash at 30 September 2026. Sarosh has told Sudarshan the Series C conversation needs the Dubai logo by the January board meeting; Sudarshan has not said whether he agrees.

At 11.40 p.m. Sanchita closed the running prototype, then opened it again to see how long the reconciliation screen took against forty suppliers of seeded data. Four hundred milliseconds. In Lohagarh's fork the same query, over real contracts, takes nine seconds. She thought about Sabiha's two questions, about the truest-feeling thing Lagori had built being also the least true, and about the board wanting one number. The one number she had was 1,420 words long, and she had written it herself.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. What did the Lathe build demonstrate, and to whom? Separate what Exhibit 3 measures from the claim Sameer makes on it.
  2. Exhibits 3 and 4 point in opposite directions. Which population matters here, and what would Lagori have had to measure, and when, for either exhibit to settle it?
  3. Exhibit 2 reports that 11 per cent of generated lines survived review, while Exhibit 5 buys ₹30.2 lakh of Lathe seats on Paths A and C regardless. What is the prototype worth, and on whose ledger does that value appear?
  4. How much of Monday's choice set was fixed in 2021, and what would it cost to reverse that decision rather than route around it again?
  5. Each path in Section 8 implies a theory of what the pilot is for. State the three. Is any of them a decision rule — and if Lagori ran Path A, what result on what date would tell it to stop?
  6. Sameer's board line and Simran's correction use the same two figures: which framing should reach the sub-committee, and who decides? It is now Monday morning — what does Sanchita do, in what order, and what does she say to the board about what the prototype has proved, what it has not, and what she needs by when to find out?

AI-generated prototypes: what a prompt builds, and what it proves

Discovery & Design › Solution Design & Prototyping — near-expert treatment

1. Two decisions in October 2026

On the afternoon of Friday, 9 October 2026, Lavanya Eranki sat in a meeting room in Madhapur, Hyderabad, with two spreadsheets and a laptop running software that had not existed three days earlier. Swasti Clinic Cloud sells outpatient-department workflow software to hospital chains, and its flagship prospect — a nine-hospital, 390-bed group across Telangana and Andhra Pradesh — would decide a three-year licence worth ₹1.38 crore, or ₹46 lakh a year, at a clinical-systems committee on Friday, 6 November, the last working Friday before the Diwali break. The contested piece was one screen: the OPD triage queue, which decides whose name the duty doctor sees next.

On Tuesday, 6 October, an engineer had fed a 1,900-word prompt — the module's wireframes, the chain's escalation policy, two pages of field notes — into a hosted generative app builder, and in under two hours had a running application: queue, filters, patient drawer, vitals panel, escalation badge. It looked better than anything the team had hand-built in two years. The spreadsheets were why Lavanya was not relieved. Lipika Erravelli, the clinical safety lead, and Likhita Edassery, the principal engineer, had audited the build against the 33 invariants the prompt specified. Seventeen were right; the other sixteen were the problem, and their shape was worse than their count.

Four days earlier and 570 kilometres away, on Monday, 5 October, Lohit Ekkirala faced the mirror image. Product lead for supply at Sangrah Market, a Bengaluru marketplace for second-hand appliances and furniture with 11,40,000 monthly active users in September 2026, he had four incompatible theories about one number: that month 1,71,000 of the 11,40,000 monthly actives (15.0 per cent) began a listing and 68,400 of those 1,71,000 finished one, a completion rate of 40.0 per cent. Twenty working days remained to the roadmap lock. The old arithmetic put one tested concept in that window; the new arithmetic put four, provided generation ran ahead of the sessions and a second researcher moderated.

Both had the same new capability and opposite exposures to it. Lohit could afford a cheap, weak instrument because a stronger one waited in his traffic. Lavanya had one buyer, one committee date and no traffic, so the artefact would carry the decision's whole evidentiary weight — the situation in which it is least trustworthy. That asymmetry, not any property of the tools, is what a manager must learn to read.

2. The idea, and the quarrel it inherited

A prototype, in the craft sense that predates all of this, is an artefact built to answer a question, characterised as much by what it deliberately fakes as by what it faithfully shows. An AI-generated prototype is one whose interactive surface — and increasingly its data layer, routing and glue logic — is produced by a generative model from a specification in words or pictures rather than authored by hand. Three kinds share the name and prove different things: a static comp, with no behaviour; front-end code running against stubbed data, which behaves while nothing behind it is real; and a full-stack application with a live data store, authentication and a public URL. The trouble lives in the third, indistinguishable from a product by every test a non-engineer can apply.

The mechanism matters the way an engine's does to a driver. These models predict continuations over an enormous corpus of published application code and interface convention, so they are excellent at the median published treatment of a described screen and weak at whatever your situation needs that is not in that median. A list with filters, pagination and a detail drawer is among the most written artefacts in software history and comes out well. A triage ordering rule encoding one chain's escalation policy exists nowhere in that corpus and comes out as a plausible list sorted on arrival time, the policy quietly absent. Hence the convention gradient: generation quality falls as the distance between your intent and the statistical centre of published software rises, and the fall is invisible in the artefact.

The idea arrived into a half-century-old argument. Frederick Brooks told managers in 1975 to plan to throw one away and by 1995 had recanted in favour of incremental growth. Barry Boehm's spiral model (1986) made prototyping an instrument of risk reduction, which his heirs read as a rule: build the artefact that retires the largest current risk, and no more. Human-computer interaction pulled the other way. Marc Rettig's "Prototyping for tiny fingers" (1994) argued for paper because paper invites criticism; Bill Buxton's Sketching User Experiences (2007) separated the sketch — suggestive, disposable — from the prototype, which is didactic and specific. Stephanie Houde and Charles Hill's "What do prototypes prototype?" (1997) gave the frame the generative era needs most: every prototype takes independent positions on role, look and feel and implementation, and confusion follows when a team forgets which dimension its artefact is strong on. Lim, Stolterman and Tenenberg (2008) added the prototype as filter: its value lies in what it omits.

Against that inheritance the schools disagree in ways worth stating as propositions, because each will sign some and refuse others.

  1. The fidelity realists. Behaviour is where learning lives; ten minutes inside running software reveals friction no mock will surface. They sign: "an artefact that runs beats an artefact that is explained." They will not sign: "generated code is a reasonable foundation for production."
  2. The sketch defenders. Finish suppresses candour. They sign: "any artefact good enough to approve is too good to critique." They will not sign: "low fidelity settles an interaction-dense flow."
  3. The spec monists. Generation being cheap, the artefact should replace the document: prompt plus running build is the specification, ambiguity settled by looking. They sign: "any requirement not visible in the artefact is not a requirement." They will not sign — their exposure — "the artefact can carry requirements that cannot be seen," where latency budgets, audit trails, retention rules and failure semantics live.
  4. The risk-first camp, Boehm's heirs, refusing all three absolutisms. They sign: "choose the lowest fidelity that can falsify the claim you are making, and name the claim first."
  5. The abstainers, found in regulated and safety-critical work. They sign: "no real personal data enters a prototype, ever, and no generated artefact is shown to a buyer as a depiction of how the product will work." Lipika Erravelli holds this position.

3. Mechanics in depth

Expert practice has a shape, and most of it happens before anything is generated. Each step exists because skipping it produces a specific failure later.

First, write the decision rule, then the prompt. A usable rule names the population the finding will be claimed over, the measure, the threshold, the sample, and the action on each side. Lohit's rule for the week of 5 October named sellers who had listed in the past ninety days, eight moderated sessions a concept, task completion and the number of participants who asked for help at least once as the measures, at most two concepts carried into a live experiment — and then the clause that is the whole of the craft: no concept would be built from this week alone. Declaring in advance what an instrument may decide is what turns a weak one into an honest one.

Second, write the filter — what the artefact will fake — before the prompt. Authentication, payments, latency, data volume, permissions, multi-tenancy, error semantics, offline behaviour. Experts put that list beside the artefact in every session, because an unwritten filter becomes an unnoticed promise.

Third, structure the prompt as domain nouns and invariants, then flow, then stubs, then states. The usual prompt describes screens; a good one describes the objects and the rules they must obey, because rules are what the convention gradient eats. The last step is the one most often left implicit: the median published interface shows the happy path, so the model shows you the happy path, and every other state must be demanded by name. Structured critique asks, for each Houde–Hill dimension, what the artefact claims and what the session evidenced, then asks what would have to be true to keep the current flow.

4. When it applies, and when it misleads

The conditions are best stated as claims checkable before a prompt is written, and each lands differently on the two protagonists.

Claim one: the question is about behaviour at the surface, not a rule beneath it. Sangrah's question — do sellers understand what to photograph first — is a surface question, which a generated artefact answers well. Swasti's — does the queue order patients as the escalation policy requires — is a rule question, which it answers badly while appearing to answer it. Claim two: a stronger instrument exists downstream. Sangrah has 1,71,000 listing-starts a month, or 5,700 a day, so the 519 participants a three-arm test needs arrive in 519 ⁄ 5,700 = 0.091 of a day, a little over two hours of traffic. That test is not cheap to build — it needs production implementations of both challengers — but it is far cheaper per unit of certainty, which is what makes the prototype week's weakness affordable. Swasti has one prospect and no traffic, so the prototype's weakness is the decision's weakness. Claim three: the audience will not mistake the artefact for a commitment. A seller recruited for an hour will not; a committee voting ₹1.38 crore will.

Where the technique actively misleads is worth naming without hedging. It misleads when the thing under test is a model's judgement rather than an interface, since a generated shell around a stubbed intelligence shows only that the shell is pleasant. It misleads when the binding risk is liquidity, which no artefact can prototype. It misleads when the question is cost of change at scale, invisible in any artefact and especially in one nobody has read. And it misleads whenever a convincing surface is taken as evidence about the interior — the Swasti case.

5. Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

In a regulated setting the danger is partly documentary: a generated build imitating a clinical workflow looks like a design record but has no author, no rationale and no traceability to a requirement, and "the model produced it" will not answer an auditor asking why the queue ordered patients as it did. India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 adds the sharper constraint — seeding a prototype with real records is a processing activity like any other, and prototypes are the systems with no retention rule, no access control and an unknown hosting location.

In multi-product companies the seam is shared infrastructure: a generated artefact quietly reinvents the identity, billing or permissions model three other products already own, so it tests an experience the platform cannot deliver — which is why mature firms generate against a stub of the real platform. In two-sided and platform situations the artefact can simulate one side completely and the other's existence not at all; the mature move is an artefact for the side in question and a concierge arrangement for the other, and the moral hazard is that a fake side is now so easy to skin convincingly that teams skip the human work that made Wizard-of-Oz honest. In hardware-plus-software work the sequence inverts: the surface can be generated months before the device exists, so teams validate interactions against an idealised sensor with no latency, drift or failure mode. In AI-native products the prototype that matters is an evaluation set, not a screen.

At the seams, what mature companies do diverges from what they say. They say the prototype is disposable. What happens is that a working artefact with a URL acquires stakeholders, and the engineering manager who inherits it chooses between rebuilding and shipping something that already demonstrably works, against a date set because the artefact appeared early. Sanrachna Build Cloud, in section 8, is that going wrong. Firms that handle it well make disposal a dated, assigned task and keep generated prototypes where production deployment is technically impossible rather than merely discouraged.

6. The nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

The prompt is the asset; the code is exhaust. The tell is the folder: versioned prompts and a build log, not branches of generated code someone has begun to maintain. The obvious reading — code is the valuable output, because code ran — is wrong because generated code's value decays once the next generation is better, while a prompt that captures a domain's invariants transfers between tools.

Fidelity is three dials, not one. The expert says unprompted which of role, look-and-feel and implementation is deliberately low; the tell is "this is fake on purpose." The obvious reading — higher fidelity is more realistic and so better — collapses as soon as an audience draws implementation conclusions from look-and-feel evidence, which is what a generated build invites.

The filter is the design. Experts write what the artefact does not do before what it does, and read the list aloud at the start of every session; the tell is a one-page annex pinned beside the screen. The obvious reading is defensive paperwork. In fact it is the only thing that keeps the artefact's evidentiary scope attached to it as it travels to people who never met it.

They price the cycle in research hours, not build hours. The tell is a plan with more concepts, fewer participants each, and a sentence naming the power knowingly given up. The obvious reading — cheaper builds mean cheaper learning — fails on Exhibit 2: once the unchanged line rises from 23.8 to 58.7 per cent of cycle cost, research capacity is the only thing worth buying.

They separate a screening instrument from a deciding one, and refuse to use the first as the second. The tell is a decision rule that names the second instrument. The obvious reading is that a vivid running artefact watched by real users is strong evidence; section 8's Fisher calculation shows a 37.5-point gap sitting at a two-sided p of 0.315.

They distrust the artefact most where it is most convincing. The expert asks of a beautiful screen which domain rule it has silently replaced; the competent practitioner asks whether the spacing is right. The tell is the order of probing: experts go first to the hardest screen that came out fastest, speed on a hard screen being the signature of substitution rather than skill.

They read the generated code — not to maintain it, but as a transcript of assumptions. This cuts against the advice to ignore the output and iterate by prompt. The tell is that the expert can name an assumption nobody asked for: a default sort, an implicit tenancy model, a rounding rule, a retry policy. You are not reviewing an implementation; you are interrogating a witness about what it thought you meant.

They generate a second artefact on purpose: the written rule table. Because the prototype's second audience is the engineer who must build the real thing, the expert ships an invariants annex stating the rules in prose and arithmetic — the parts the artefact cannot carry. The tell is a handover pack of two documents, neither a screenshot. The obvious reading, that the prototype is the specification and a document redundant, is the proposition the spec monists cannot defend: latency budgets, audit trails and retention rules are invisible by construction, the last failure mode in section 9.

7. How this differs across product types and company stages

In consumer products with traffic the generated prototype is a candidate generator and almost never a decider, the decider being a live experiment that is cheaper per unit of certainty. In B2B and enterprise the ordering reverses: there is no traffic, the prototype often is the evidence, and it becomes a quasi-commitment, because a buyer who has clicked through it believes they have seen the product. That double role — instrument and promise — is the defining enterprise difficulty, and why enterprise teams invest in the filter annex consumer teams can skip. In platforms and marketplaces one side can be prototyped and liquidity cannot; in hardware the software surface generates and the physical affordance does not; in AI products a generated interface over a stubbed model is an elaborate way of learning nothing.

By stage: pre-seed, the artefact is the pitch and the risk is self-deception, the founder being both generator and audience. At growth stage it competes against a live experiment and loses on evidence while winning on speed, so the honest use is sequencing — prototype to choose what to test, test to decide. At scale the risks turn organisational: promotion of the artefact, procurement commitments, and the regression of the product's distinctiveness toward the model's priors. Where the difference is not real, say so: decision rule, filter list, seed-data discipline and frozen build apply identically at every stage.

Sanrachna Build Cloud: the failure, and what recovery cost

In 2024 Sanrachna Build Cloud, an Ahmedabad firm selling site-progress software to construction contractors, generated a field-inspection module in three days, demoed it to a prospect who signed, and — under a date set by the demo — shipped the generated code with light cleanup. The surface was genuinely good. The interior carried an assumption nobody had asked for and nobody had read: a single-tenant data model in which a project's records implicitly belonged to one customer. Nine months and fourteen customers later the re-platforming took five engineers eleven weeks — 55 engineer-weeks, or 275 engineer-days at ₹12,000, which is ₹33 lakh. Designing the data model before generating the surface was afterwards estimated at 16 engineer-weeks, 80 days, or ₹9.6 lakh. The excess was ₹23.4 lakh, and two renewals slipped a quarter.

The recovery is the useful part, and it was not "they rebuilt everything." They kept the generated interface, the real gift of the technique, and rebuilt the data layer behind it: eleven weeks of work with no visible change for customers. The lesson the team now gives every new hire is one sentence — the surface was an asset and the interior a liability, and the mistake was treating them as one object to accept or reject together.

9. Failure modes, with their early warning signs

Silent substitution of a domain rule by a convention. Early sign: the hard screen came out faster and more complete than the easy one. Diagnostic: "show me where rule X is enforced, then change rule X and show me the artefact change." Late cost: Swasti's ₹9.87 lakh exposure, and in clinical use worse than money. The median-data illusion. Early sign: seed data with no duplicates, no missing fields, no absurd records. Diagnostic: "what does the 99th-percentile row look like, and what does this screen do with it?" Promotion of the prototype. Early sign: somebody asks for repository access. Diagnostic: "what would it cost to delete this on Friday?" — any answer but "nothing" means it is already production. Finish-induced approval. Early sign: reviews produce approvals and colour comments rather than objections. Diagnostic: "what are we not asking you about?"

Convention regression. Early sign: the artefact looks like every competitor's, the model's priors being the industry's average. Diagnostic: "which element could a competitor not copy by Friday?" Build drift. Early sign: two researchers describe different behaviour from what both call "the prototype." Diagnostic: "which build did participant six see?" The forking garden. Early sign: concepts tested rose and pre-registered decision rules did not. Diagnostic: "what result would have made us keep the current flow?" Compliance leakage. Early sign: "I pulled a small extract to make it realistic." Diagnostic: "whose data is in this build, on what basis, hosted where?" Loss of the engineering cost veto. Early sign: estimates arrive after designs are approved. Diagnostic: "what does this screen cost per month at ten times today's volume?" Invisible requirements dropped. Early sign: the written specification quietly stopped being updated. Diagnostic: "where is the latency budget, the audit trail, the retention rule?"

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Does high fidelity improve or corrupt feedback? The realists note that friction lives in behaviour, and that the comparative-fidelity studies of the 1990s — Virzi, Sokolov and Karis (1996), Catani and Biers (1998) — are generally read as finding broadly similar problem-detection counts for paper and computer prototypes: if fidelity does not change detection, take the richer artefact. The defenders answer that those studies counted problems, not candour, and that finish changes the kind of comment, moving a session from "what if it worked differently" to "the label is wrong." For the realists to be wrong, generated finish would have to suppress discovery of structural alternatives; for the defenders to be wrong, participants would have to object structurally to finished artefacts as readily as to rough ones. Neither is established.

Is generated code a legitimate production seed? The affirmative case is stronger than it is given credit for: all code is a liability, the comparison is against what a rushed human would have written to the same deadline, and a codebase that ships beats one that is pure. The negative case rests on the cost-of-change curve — Sanrachna's ₹23.4 lakh excess — and on nobody having read the thing, so its assumptions are unknown rather than merely bad. Settling it needs public evidence on defect density and change cost at twelve and twenty-four months, which does not exist in a form anyone should bet a company on.

Does cheap prototyping raise or lower learning per rupee? The optimists have Exhibit 2 and the point that four shots beat one. The pessimists have a better argument than they are usually allowed: the binding constraint was never the cost of the artefact but the quality of the question, and cheapening the artefact lets a team skip question formulation, so artefacts per rupee rise while learning per rupee falls. Exhibit 1's first column is their exhibit too.

Who should hold the prompt? One camp says the product manager, the prompt being the specification and specification the job; another the designer, because an untrained hand produces convention regression; a third the engineer, because only they will notice the implicit tenancy model. This is an organisational question in a craft question's clothes, and the three camps optimise different real risks.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this generates quickly and shows the result. Someone who has internalised it states, before generating, what the artefact will be allowed to decide; is more suspicious of their best-looking screens than of their worst; talks about research capacity rather than build capacity when asked what is slowing discovery; and is comfortable deleting a working application on a Friday afternoon, never having confused the artefact with the knowledge it bought.

12. The decisions, and three questions

Lohit Ekkirala decided on 13 October not to build anything. He carried C and B into a live three-arm test against the current flow at 173 per arm — 519 participants, a little over two hours of Sangrah's traffic — and wrote into the roadmap note that the prototype week had produced candidates and explanations, not a result. An instrument whose largest observed gap carries a two-sided p of 0.315 is a screening device, and he owned a better one.

Lavanya Eranki decided to show the 16 October build to the chain's clinicians on 23 October, but to change what it was called and what travelled with it. It would be presented as a workflow sketch, not a module; the filter annex listing what it faked would be read aloud at the start; and the triage ordering rule — the four silently replaced invariants — would be lifted out of the artefact into a one-page rule table with worked examples, which the clinicians would review as arithmetic rather than as a screen. With one instrument and no downstream test, the only way to make it honest was to shrink its claims to what it could support.

  1. The audit found 12 of 33 invariants silently replaced. Had it found twelve visibly missing and nothing silently replaced, how should Lavanya's 23 October decision change — and what does that tell you about which kind of prototype you would rather hold?
  2. Lohit's week cost ₹2.36 lakh for four concepts at ₹58,900 each and produced no defensible comparison. Build the strongest case that it was waste, then that it was his quarter's best fortnight. Which argument depends on facts you do not have?
  3. Sanrachna kept the generated surface and rebuilt the interior. When would the opposite recovery be right, and what would you need to know about the generation step to tell in advance?

13. Going deeper

  • Wireframes, mockups, prototypes. The vocabulary this depends on: without it a generated build cannot be placed on Houde and Hill's dimensions, and Figure 1's belief gap stays invisible.
  • The prototype as the new specification. The contested consequence: which requirements can live inside an artefact, and which must still be written down.
  • Writing a solution hypothesis. What makes a decision rule possible; a prompt with no hypothesis behind it yields an artefact with nothing to falsify.
  • Ideation: brainstorming, Crazy 8s, HMW. Now the binding upstream constraint: the generated path consumes four concepts a window and most teams cannot produce four different ones.
  • Concept and elevator pitch. The compression test a concept must survive before it earns a prompt, and the cheapest guard against convention regression.
  • Value Proposition Canvas. Where the invariants come from: jobs, pains and gains are the raw material of the rule list the convention gradient otherwise replaces.
  • Value proposition statement. The sentence a generated artefact cannot write for you, and what a buyer's enthusiasm for a demo most often obscures.
  • Storyboarding. The role dimension in narrative form; it holds the argument on what the product is for while a beautiful screen pulls it toward look-and-feel.

AI-generated prototypes

What a prompt can build in an afternoon, what that build proves, and what it never will.

1. Opening: a demo that was too good

On Monday 9 March 2026, Kavitha Dandekar, Director of Product at Ruvanta Credit, a Pune-based digital lender, spent her morning typing. Her team had been discussing for two quarters a feature called Salary Bridge: an advance of up to half a month's pay for salaried borrowers, requested in the app and repaid automatically on payday. By lunchtime, working from a written description of the screens and a list of rules, she had a clickable version running on her phone. By Wednesday it had been refined with a designer, older mock-ups pasted in as reference, and run past four colleagues. On Friday 13 March she was due to show it to the leadership committee, which would decide whether to commit five engineers for twelve weeks.

The arithmetic of that decision was sobering. Five people for twelve weeks is 60 person-weeks. Ruvanta budgets a loaded cost of ₹1.5 lakh per person-week, so the build would cost 60 × 1.5 = ₹90 lakh. A conventional clickable prototype, made by a designer and an engineer over three weeks, would have been 2 × 3 = 6 person-weeks, or ₹9 lakh. Kavitha's version had taken three person-days, which at five working days to the week is 0.6 person-weeks, or ₹0.90 lakh. Cheap and fast, then. The risk was the opposite of the usual one. The prototype looked so finished that the committee might treat it as evidence the product existed, and Kishor Dharmadhikari, her lead engineer, had already warned her that "it demos beautifully because nothing in it is real."

This page follows her decision. The question it answers is a practical one: can a prompt produce a working prototype, and what does that prototype prove and not prove? The argument runs in one line from start to finish. An AI-generated prototype makes the asking of a question nearly free; it does not make the answer free, and the whole skill lies in knowing which question you have bought.

2. The idea

An AI-generated prototype is an interactive artefact, produced by giving a generative model a written description of what you want, that is good enough to put in front of a person and watch what they do. A prompt is simply that description: the user, the task, the screens, the rules, the tone. A prototype is a model of a product built to answer a question before the real product is built. The older vocabulary matters here. A wireframe is a schematic of layout; a mock-up is a static picture of finished appearance; a prototype is the first of the three that responds to a touch. The new element is who does the building. Before, the cost of an interactive artefact was weeks of a specialist's time; with generative models able to write the interface code from a description, the cost falls to hours of anyone who can describe the product clearly.

The underlying problem is old. Product teams have long sought some way to learn from users before paying for engineering, and the practice of prototype, critique, revise predates the current models by decades. Rapid prototyping tools, the design sprint method, developed at Google around 2010 and published by Google Ventures around 2016, and lean start-up thinking of the same period all attacked the same waste: building the wrong thing at full price. Generative models, which became capable of producing working interface code from prose in the early 2020s, did not change the purpose. They changed the price of a turn of the loop.

Kavitha's repeatable sentence, the one she could say in the committee without sounding glib, was this: "The prototype tells us whether people can do the task and want to; it tells us nothing about whether we can deliver it, so I am asking for a decision on the first half only." Notice that the sentence assigns the prototype a job. That assignment is the idea.

3. How it actually works

The mechanics have six steps, and practitioners usually leave the first and the last implicit.

Step one is to state the question and the decision rule before touching the tool. Kavitha wrote: "Can a salaried borrower request an advance unaided in under four minutes, and will at least 14 of 20 test users (70 per cent) do so?" Without that sentence, a prototype becomes an object of admiration rather than a measurement. Step two is the prompt itself. Hers named the user (a salaried borrower earning between ₹25,000 and ₹60,000 a month), the task, the five screens, the eligibility rule (an advance of up to 50 per cent of monthly salary), the fee display and the failure messages. Step three is generation. Step four is the one most people shortcut: inspecting the output against the question, not against taste. She asked of each screen what the user must decide, and whether the prototype had silently decided it for them.

The loop from inspection back to the prompt is the technique's real gift. When something is wrong, the discipline is to change the description and regenerate, not to patch the output by hand, because the prompt becomes a record of the decisions made. Step five is a test with real users, with the number stated beforehand. Step six is to decide by the rule you wrote at the start. The dashed arrow records a further possibility: sometimes the test shows that the question itself was wrong.

4. A worked example

Kavitha tested with 20 salaried borrowers recruited from Ruvanta's existing customers, each given the same task and a stopwatch. Sixteen completed the advance request unaided and inside four minutes. That is 16 of 20, or 80 per cent, against a rule of 14 of 20, or 70 per cent. On its face, the rule was cleared by two people.

The second reading is more careful. With n = 20 and 16 successes, the 95 per cent Wilson interval for the true completion rate runs from about 58 per cent to 92 per cent. The rule's threshold of 70 per cent sits inside that interval, so the test does not show the true rate is above 70; it shows it is plausible. A sample of twenty is adequate for finding usability problems and inadequate for estimating a rate precisely, and Kavitha resolved to say so before anyone repeated "80 per cent" in the committee room.

Now change one input. Kishor pointed out that the prototype showed the verification step as always succeeding, because the model had been told to fake a successful result. In the real app, only 4,200 of 6,000 applicants, 70 per cent, pass verification on their first attempt. Someone who fails can retry, but a retry costs time and would probably breach the four-minute limit, so 0.56 is best read as a floor on unaided first-pass completion, not as a forecast of eventual completion. Two assumptions sit under the multiplication: that the rates are independent, and that the 6,000 live applicants resemble the 20 recruited existing customers, who may well have tidier documents. On those assumptions the first-pass completion is 0.80 × 0.70 = 0.56, or 11.2 of 20 users, and the rule is not met. Raise first-attempt verification to 90 per cent through better document capture, and the product becomes 0.80 × 0.90 = 0.72, or 14.4 of 20, which clears it.

The figure shows why the same prototype supports two opposite decisions. The interface, the part the prompt could build, was never the weak link. The weak link was a dependency the prototype pretended away. Kavitha therefore reframed her request: not "approve the build" but "approve the build conditional on a verification fix, and fund that fix first."

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

A prototype is a question, not a miniature product

People say "minimum viable product" loosely. In the better programmes, a prototype or a minimum viable product is defined as a learning vehicle with a decision rule attached: a thing built to produce a specific piece of evidence. A small product that no one has agreed how to judge teaches nothing, however polished.

Plausible is not feasible

A model will write an interface that behaves as if a salary-verification service, a payments rail and a credit engine all exist. It costs nothing to claim a capability in code that talks to nothing. The test is to ask, of every behaviour on screen, "what real system would have to answer this?" and to list those systems.

The defaults are decisions nobody made

The model fills every gap in your prompt with something reasonable: a fee label, an error message, a sort order. These defaults then look like design. Reading the output for what you did not specify is the fastest way to find unmade decisions, and a cheap source of them is to ask the model to list the assumptions it made.

Prototype, wireframe and MVP are different instruments

A wireframe answers "is the structure sensible?" A prototype answers "can a person do the task?" An MVP, in the sense of a real product with a few real customers, answers "will people use and pay for it, and can we operate it?" Substituting an earlier instrument for a later one is the commonest error. The prototype builds the thing the wireframe describes; it does not stand in for the thing the market decides.

Users rehearse the happy path

Test users given a seeded, tidy scenario succeed in a tidy way. Real borrowers arrive with blurred documents, expired passwords and a bank holiday. The prototype can be prompted to produce failures, and should be; the cheapest improvement to any test is to give two of the twenty a deliberately broken scenario.

Stated preference is not behaviour

A user who says "yes, I would use this" in front of a good-looking screen is giving the weakest form of evidence. Prototypes can show whether someone can use the feature and what they say; they cannot show whether they will come back in week six, whether they will repay, or whether the economics work. Those need live exposure of real money or real time.

The same prompt is not the same result

Generative output varies from run to run. Treat the prompt, with a date and the tool's identity, as the source document, and expect to regenerate. Do not claim a result depends on a screen you cannot reproduce.

The code is a sketch, not a foundation

Generated interface code can be reused, but it has seen no security review, no accessibility testing, no load. Treating it as the beginning of production is a decision that must be taken on purpose, with engineering, not discovered by default.

6. How it differs by product type and company stage

In consumer products, the prototype's strength is speed through many variants: five onboarding flows can be generated and shown to a dozen users each in a week. The risk is the illusion of habit, since a single session says nothing about retention. In business-to-business products, the buyer and the user differ, and a prototype can be put in front of both; the weakness is integration. Customers care about how the product meets their existing systems, which no generated screen displays. In marketplaces, a prototype can show one side's experience but cannot simulate liquidity: whether a seller sees buyers, or a rider gets a job within minutes, depends on the other side being present in numbers.

Early-stage companies use these prototypes to replace most of the early specification: the prototype is shown to investors, customers and engineers, and often is the specification. Large firms gain differently, because they can afford a prototype for every proposal in the portfolio. Their danger is governance: a hundred persuasive prototypes make a worse queue than a hundred bullet lists unless each carries its question and rule.

7. Common mistakes

Mistaking polish for proof. The symptom is a committee that says "looks done, why is it taking twelve weeks?" The misunderstanding is that appearance indicates progress. The cheapest diagnostic is to put the list of unreal dependencies on the first slide.

Hand-editing the output until nobody can reproduce it. The symptom is a prototype no one on the team can change, because the prompt that made it is gone. The misunderstanding is that the artefact is the deliverable. The diagnostic: can a colleague regenerate it in an hour from the saved prompt?

Testing without a rule. The symptom is sessions that end with "people liked it." The misunderstanding is that observation is conclusion. The diagnostic: ask what result would have made you stop, and if nobody can say, the test cannot change anything.

Quoting a rate from a small sample. The symptom is "80 per cent succeeded" repeated without the 20. The misunderstanding is that a percentage describes the population when it describes only the sample. The diagnostic is to write the n and the interval beside the number.

8. What good looks like

The same decision handled well looks like this. A one-page brief states the question, the rule (14 of 20 unaided in four minutes), the list of faked dependencies and the single riskiest one. The prototype is generated from a saved prompt. Test sessions include broken scenarios. The number shown to the committee is "16 of 20, interval 58 to 92 per cent, with verification faked; 11.2 of 20 on a first-pass basis with the live success rate." The request that follows is sized to the evidence: a ₹30 lakh verification project (5 people, 4 weeks) ahead of a ₹90 lakh build.

The committee approved not the ₹90 lakh build but a four-week verification project of 5 people for 4 weeks, 20 person-weeks at ₹1.5 lakh, or ₹30 lakh, with the build contingent on first-attempt verification reaching 90 per cent. Her reasoning was that the prototype had bought a cheap, honest answer about the interface and a cheap, uncomfortable answer about what to fund next.

What to learn next is the prototype as a specification, since a working artefact can be handed to engineers as the statement of what to build, and with it come new questions about what in a prototype is intended and what is incidental.

Two questions to sit with. Which of your own current product beliefs would survive if the prototype that supported them had been generated with every dependency made to fail? And what decision rule, written in advance, would you be willing to be held to?
